# Design a Web Search Engine (Google)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Google • Bing` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Crawling is a data-collection problem, but search is a two-part problem in disguise: build an **inverted index** big enough that no single machine can hold it, then **rank** matching documents well enough that the ten blue links on page one are actually the right ten, and those two concerns need almost entirely separate systems.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a web search engine: given billions of crawled web pages, let a user
type a query and get back a ranked list of the most relevant pages in well
under a second. You can assume crawling is a separate, already-solved
system; focus on how the crawled pages become a searchable, ranked index
and how a single query gets served fast against it.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How large is the corpus, roughly how many web pages are we indexing?
*Why it matters:* Tens of billions of pages means the index cannot live on one machine under any design; it decides, immediately, that this is a sharded, distributed-index problem rather than a 'build a search library' problem.

#### Q: Do we need to rank by relevance and authority, or is returning any matching set of documents enough?
*Why it matters:* Boolean matching (does the term appear) is a solved, cheap problem. Ranking millions of matches down to the best ten, blending link authority with text relevance, is the actual hard problem this interview is testing.

#### Q: How fresh does the index need to be, can we tolerate pages being a day stale, or does breaking news need to appear in minutes?
*Why it matters:* A daily batch-rebuilt index is far cheaper to build than one supporting near-real-time incremental updates; freshness requirements directly decide the indexing pipeline's architecture.

#### Q: Should we support just single keywords, or also phrases, boolean operators, and typo tolerance?
*Why it matters:* Phrase queries need positional information stored in the index, not just term presence, which meaningfully increases index size and changes the index's data structure.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can submit a free-text query and receive a ranked list of matching web pages.
- Results must include a title and a short snippet showing the query terms in context.
- The system supports multi-word queries, treating them as an implicit AND over relevant terms plus phrase proximity boosting.
- The index is continuously (or at least periodically) updated as new pages are crawled and old ones change or disappear.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Query latency must be well under a second end to end, ideally under 200ms, since search is the single most latency-sensitive product surface there is.**
- **The system must scale to tens of billions of documents and hundreds of thousands of queries per second at peak, globally.**
- **High availability: search must degrade gracefully (serve from a slightly stale index) rather than go down, since downtime on search is directly visible to hundreds of millions of users.**
- **Ranking quality matters as much as raw availability, a fast search engine that returns bad results has effectively failed its purpose.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50 billion web pages in the corpus
- Average page has 1,000 unique meaningful terms after stripping stopwords
- 3.5 billion queries per day globally
- Each posting (a term's reference to one document) takes roughly 8 bytes once compressed (doc ID + position/frequency info)

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Raw postings in the index:** 50,000,000,000 pages * 1,000 terms/page = 50 trillion postings total across the whole inverted index
- **Compressed index size:** 50 trillion postings * 8 bytes ≈ 400 TB, which is far beyond any single machine's RAM or disk, forcing horizontal sharding across thousands of index-serving machines
- **Query throughput:** 3,500,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 40,500 queries/sec average, with peak traffic commonly 3-5x that, so design for roughly 150,000-200,000 queries/sec at peak
- **Per-shard load at 200ms budget:** If the index is split across 10,000 shards, each shard handles ~15-20 queries/sec at peak, comfortably servable from RAM if each shard's slice of the index fits in memory on its machine

*Capacity Takeaway:* The index is ==two to three orders of magnitude larger than any single machine can hold==, so **sharding** the inverted index across thousands of machines is not an optimization, it's the only way this system can exist at all, and every other design decision (query fan-out, ranking, caching) follows from that one fact.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Offline, a batch pipeline turns crawled pages into two things: an inverted
index (term -> sorted postings list of documents containing it, sharded
across thousands of machines by term) and a per-document authority score
computed from the link graph via a PageRank-style algorithm. Online, a
query comes into a stateless query-serving tier, which tokenizes the query,
fans it out in parallel to every index shard that could hold a matching
term, each shard returns its best local matches with a partial relevance
score, and an aggregator merges those partial result sets, blends in each
document's precomputed authority score, and returns the final top-ranked
page. Because the corpus and index are both far larger than one machine can
hold, both the indexing pipeline and the query-serving path are
distributed by construction, not as a later optimization.

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    crawler["Crawled Pages"]:::server
    indexer["Indexing Pipeline"]:::server
    pagerank["PageRank Job"]:::server
    shards["Sharded Inverted Index"]:::server
    docstore[("Document Store")]:::db
    client["Client"]:::client
    gateway["Query Gateway"]:::server
    aggregator["Query Aggregator"]:::server
    crawler -->|"parsed pages"| indexer

    indexer -.->|"build postings"| shards
    pagerank -.->|"authority scores"| docstore
    client --> gateway
    gateway --> aggregator
    aggregator -->|"scatter query"| shards
    shards -->|"top-K matches"| aggregator
    aggregator -->|"fetch title/snippet"| docstore
```

    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Each shard scores local matches (BM25-style relevance)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Gather and merge (aggregator combines top-K per shard)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Blend authority score (precomputed PageRank-style score)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Return ranked results (with title + snippet)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search` | Query params: q (search string), page (result page number). Returns a ranked, paginated list of results, each with url, title, snippet, and score. |
| `GET` | `/api/search/suggest` | Query param: q (partial query). Returns a short list of autocomplete suggestions, backed by a separate, much smaller, prefix-indexed query-log store. |
| `POST` | `/internal/index/document` | Internal-only. Called by the indexing pipeline to submit a newly crawled or re-crawled page's parsed content for indexing. |
| `DELETE` | `/internal/index/document/{docId}` | Internal-only. Removes a page from the index, called when a crawl detects a 404 or a page has been deindexed for policy reasons. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `inverted_index`
- `term (string, the sharding/partition key)`
- `postings_list (ordered list of { doc_id, term_frequency, positions[] })`
*Notes:* Not a traditional row-oriented table, this is a custom on-disk/in-memory structure, term -> sorted list of documents containing it, sharded across many machines by term so each shard owns a slice of the vocabulary.

### Entity: `document_store`
- `doc_id (unique)`
- `url`
- `title`
- `raw_content (or a pointer to it in blob storage)`
- `pagerank_score (precomputed, updated periodically)`
- `last_crawled_at`
*Notes:* The source of truth for a page's content and precomputed authority score, separate from the inverted index itself, and sharded by doc_id since it's fetched by ID at result-rendering time, not searched by term.

### Entity: `link_graph`
- `from_doc_id`
- `to_doc_id`

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you rank millions of matching documents down to the best ten?
Ranking blends two very different signals. **Relevance** signals come from the document itself: how often and where query terms appear (TF-IDF or BM25-style scoring), whether they appear in the title versus buried in the body, whether they appear as an exact phrase. **Authority** signals come from the link graph, independent of any query: a PageRank-style score treats a link from page A to page B as a vote, weighted by A's own authority, computed once offline over the entire link graph and reused for every query that page shows up in. A query-time score is a weighted combination of both.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure text relevance (TF-IDF/BM25) alone: cheap to compute per query, but easily gamed by keyword-stuffed low-quality pages, and can't distinguish an authoritative page from a spam page using the same terms
- Pure link-based authority (PageRank) alone: hard to game cheaply, but ignores whether the page is actually about the query at all, an authoritative page on an unrelated topic would still rank highly for irrelevant queries
- The real answer: combine both, precompute the expensive, query-independent authority score offline once, and compute the cheap, query-dependent relevance score at query time, multiplying or blending them into a final rank

### How do you make a query fast against an index that spans thousands of machines?
A query fans out in parallel (**scatter**) to every shard that could contain a matching term, each shard computes its own top-K local matches independently using its in-memory postings list, and a query-aggregation tier merges those partial ranked lists into one final ranked list (**gather**). This scatter-gather pattern is what keeps latency flat as the corpus grows, adding more shards adds more parallel work, not more sequential work, as long as the shard count and per-shard latency stay roughly constant.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Scatter-gather across all shards: query latency is bounded by the slowest shard, not the sum of all shards, but ==a single slow or overloaded shard becomes a tail-latency problem== for every query touching it
- Mitigation: replicate each shard (multiple copies on different machines) so the aggregator can route around a slow replica, and set an aggressive per-shard timeout, returning slightly incomplete results rather than waiting on a straggler
- An alternative of routing a query to only a subset of shards (skip ones deemed unlikely to have great matches) would cut latency further, but risks silently missing a genuinely relevant document, an unacceptable trade-off for a general-purpose search engine

### How do you keep the index reasonably fresh without rebuilding all 400TB of it constantly?
A full index rebuild from scratch is a large batch job, fine for a daily cadence but far too slow for pages that change hourly or breaking news that needs to appear within minutes. Most production search systems layer a small, frequently-updated incremental index on top of a large, less frequently rebuilt base index, merging results from both at query time, then periodically folding the incremental index into a fresh base index and clearing it.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Full rebuild only: simple, one index to reason about, but freshness is bounded by how long a full rebuild takes, unacceptable for time-sensitive content
- Base index plus small incremental index, merged at query time: much fresher, but doubles query-time complexity (search two structures, merge results) and needs a periodic, carefully-ordered merge/compaction process
- This mirrors the same base-plus-delta pattern used in write-heavy log-structured storage engines, applied here to keep index rebuild cost proportional to what changed, not to the whole corpus

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single hot shard (a very common term like 'the' or a trending topic) can receive disproportionate query load; mitigate by replicating hot shards more heavily and caching their most common query results.
- The offline PageRank computation over tens of billions of nodes and their links is itself a massive distributed batch job (commonly built on a MapReduce-style framework); it doesn't need to run per query, but it does need to complete on a schedule that keeps authority scores from going stale.
- Query aggregators become a fan-in bottleneck at very high query volume; scaling them horizontally (many stateless aggregator instances behind a load balancer) and caching full result pages for extremely common queries reduces repeat scatter-gather work.
- Index shard rebalancing as the corpus grows unevenly (some terms/topics grow faster than others) requires a resharding strategy, similar in spirit to resharding a distributed key-value store, so no single shard's vocabulary grows disproportionately large.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Treating this as 'just build a big database and do a LIKE query'==, missing that full-text relevance ranking and link-based authority are the actual hard problems being tested, not storage.
- ⚠️ Proposing a single, unsharded index and only discovering during the interview that it can't physically fit on one machine at web scale.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that link authority (PageRank) must be computed offline and reused, not recomputed per query, an interviewer will immediately probe this if it's missing.
- ⚠️ Designing a query path with no timeout or fallback for a slow shard, letting one straggling machine set the latency for every query that touches it.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just build one big inverted index on one very large machine?**

> **Model Answer:** At tens of billions of documents, the compressed postings list alone runs into the hundreds of terabytes, which is orders of magnitude beyond any single machine's RAM or even fast local disk. Sharding by term is required just to make the index fit in memory across a fleet, which is also what makes scatter-gather queries fast, since each shard searches only its own in-memory slice.

**Q: Why is PageRank computed offline instead of at query time?**

> **Model Answer:** **PageRank** depends only on the link graph, not on any particular query, so its result is the same regardless of what a user searches for. Computing it once offline as a batch job and storing the resulting score alongside each document means query time only needs a cheap lookup, not a graph traversal, which would be far too slow to run per query at the required latency.

**Q: How would you prevent a single trending topic from overwhelming its index shard?**

> **Model Answer:** Detect hot shards from query-volume metrics and replicate them more heavily than average shards, spreading their query load across more machines, and add a caching layer in front of the aggregator for extremely frequent queries so identical repeated searches don't trigger a fresh scatter-gather every time.

# Design a Recommendation System

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Amazon • Netflix` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Recommending well is a slow, heavy math problem (crunching a giant user-item interaction matrix), but serving a recommendation is a fast, cheap lookup, so the entire system is really two systems glued together: an **offline pipeline** that has minutes to get the math right, and an **online path** that has milliseconds to hand back an answer it already computed.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a recommendation system: given a catalog of items (products, movies,
shows) and a history of user interactions (purchases, watches, ratings,
clicks), show each user a personalized ranked list of items they're likely
to want next. Design the system end to end, including how recommendations
get computed and how they get served fast enough for a homepage to load.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we have explicit signals (star ratings) or only implicit signals (clicks, purchases, watch time, dwell time)?
*Why it matters:* Explicit ratings are sparse but unambiguous. Implicit signals are abundant but noisy, a click isn't the same as liking something, and the modeling approach (and the loss function underneath it) differs materially between the two.

#### Q: How do we handle a brand-new user or a brand-new item with no interaction history yet?
*Why it matters:* Any model trained purely on past interactions has nothing to say about a user or item it has never seen. This cold-start gap needs its own fallback strategy, or the product breaks for every new signup and every new listing.

#### Q: Do recommendations need to update within the same session (react to what a user just clicked), or is a recommendation list refreshed once a day acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Same-session responsiveness requires a real-time or near-real-time feature and scoring path layered on top of the batch model. A daily refresh is far cheaper and lets the whole heavy computation stay offline.

#### Q: How large is the catalog, thousands of items or hundreds of millions?
*Why it matters:* A small catalog can be scored exhaustively per user. A massive catalog needs a cheap candidate-generation step to narrow the field before any expensive ranking model runs, changing the whole pipeline shape.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a user, return a ranked list of N items that user is likely to be interested in.
- The system incorporates a user's own interaction history (views, purchases, ratings) into their recommendations.
- The system can recommend reasonably relevant items for a user or item with little to no interaction history (cold start).
- Recommendations refresh as new interactions accumulate, without requiring a full model retrain for every single new click.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Serving a recommendation list must be fast, well under 100-200ms, since it's rendered on high-traffic pages like the homepage and product detail pages.**
- **The offline model-training pipeline must scale to hundreds of millions of users and tens of millions of items without needing a full pairwise comparison of all of them.**
- **High availability for serving: if the recommendation service is degraded, the product should fall back to a simple, always-available list (like 'trending now') rather than show an error or a blank page.**
- **Freshness is a tunable trade-off: the model can be retrained on a daily or hourly batch cadence, it does not need to be updated on every single interaction.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 100 million active users
- 10 million catalog items
- Average user has 50 recorded interactions (purchases, ratings, significant watches)
- Homepage recommendation widget is viewed 300 million times per day

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Size of the raw interaction matrix:** 100,000,000 users * 10,000,000 items = 10^15 possible cells, hopelessly sparse and impossible to store or compute densely
- **Actual stored interactions (sparse):** 100,000,000 users * 50 interactions = 5 billion actual interaction records, roughly a million times smaller than the dense matrix, which is why every technique here depends on exploiting sparsity
- **Serving throughput:** 300,000,000 views / 86,400 seconds ≈ 3,500 requests/sec average, spiking well higher at peak shopping/viewing hours
- **Precomputed recommendation storage:** 100,000,000 users * 100 precomputed item IDs each * 8 bytes ≈ 80 GB, comfortably fits in a distributed in-memory cache, which is exactly why precomputing offline and serving from cache is viable

*Capacity Takeaway:* The dense user-item matrix is ==computationally impossible at this scale== (10^15 cells), so every real design here hinges on exploiting **sparsity**: train offline against only the 5 billion actual interactions, precompute a small per-user recommendation list from that, and serve it as a cheap 80GB cache lookup rather than ever scoring the full catalog per user at request time.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Offline, an interaction event stream (views, clicks, purchases, ratings)
feeds a batch training pipeline that factorizes the sparse user-item matrix
into low-dimensional user and item embeddings (collaborative filtering),
augmented with item metadata features (content-based signals) for items
with too little interaction history to model collaboratively. The pipeline
writes two precomputed outputs: a per-user top-N recommendation list, and a
per-item similarity list, both pushed into a fast, distributed cache. Online,
a request for a user's recommendations is a cache read, not a
computation, an app server looks up the precomputed list, optionally
re-ranks the top candidates with cheap, real-time signals (like the current
session's clicks), and returns the result. A cold-start path falls back to
content-based similarity or catalog-wide popularity when a user or item has
no history to work from.

#### Offline training pipeline and online serving path

```mermaid

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    events>"Interaction Events"]:::queue

    trainer["Batch Training Job"]:::server
    reccache["Recommendation Cache"]:::cache
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    events -.->|"persist"| interactionsdb
    interactionsdb -->|"batch read"| trainer
    trainer -.->|"write top-N per user"| reccache

#### Collaborative filtering vs content-based filtering

| Collaborative filtering | Content-based filtering |
| :--- | :--- |
| Learns from interaction patterns across all users | Learns from item attributes and one user's own history |
| Can surface non-obvious, cross-category picks | Works immediately for new items with metadata |
| Useless for a brand-new user or item (cold start) | Limited to whatever features were actually encoded |

#### Cold-start routing decision

  b -->|"No"| c["Popularity fallback"]

  d -->|"Yes"| f["Collaborative filtering"]
  c --> g["Blend, shift weight as history grows"]
  e --> g
  f --> g
```

#### Collaborative weight vs interaction count

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/recommendations/{userId}` | Query params: context (e.g. homepage, product_page), limit. Returns a ranked list of item IDs with scores for the given user and surface. |
| `GET` | `/api/recommendations/{userId}/similar-to/{itemId}` | Returns items similar to itemId, used for 'customers also bought' style widgets, backed by item-item similarity rather than the full user model. |
| `POST` | `/internal/interactions` | Internal-only. Records a new interaction event (view, click, purchase, rating) into the event stream feeding the offline training pipeline. |
| `POST` | `/internal/models/train` | Internal-only, typically triggered by a scheduler rather than a human. Kicks off the next batch training run of the recommendation model against accumulated interaction data. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `interactions`
- `user_id (indexed)`
- `item_id (indexed)`
- `interaction_type (view, click, purchase, rating)`
- `value (rating value, or implicit weight for clicks/purchases)`
- `timestamp`
*Notes:* The raw event log, append-only, and the sole input to offline model training; sharded by user_id since most reads during training are per-user interaction history.

### Entity: `user_item_scores`
- `user_id (key)`
- `recommended_items (ordered list of { item_id, score })`
*Notes:* The precomputed output of the offline pipeline, one row per user, refreshed on each training cycle; this is what the serving path actually reads at request time, never the raw interaction log.

### Entity: `item_similarity`
- `item_id (key)`
- `similar_items (ordered list of { item_id, similarity_score })`
*Notes:* Precomputed item-item similarity, independent of any single user, used for 'similar items' widgets and as a cold-start fallback for new users based on the one or two items they've just looked at.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Collaborative filtering vs content-based filtering: the central modeling trade-off
**Collaborative filtering** learns from the pattern of interactions itself: users who behaved similarly to each other in the past will probably like similar things in the future, no knowledge of what the items actually are required. It's typically implemented as **matrix factorization**, decomposing the sparse user-item interaction matrix into a low-dimensional user embedding and item embedding whose dot product approximates affinity. **Content-based filtering** instead looks at item attributes (genre, category, price, description) and a user's own past preferences for those attributes, recommending items with similar features to what that user already liked, no data about other users required at all.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Collaborative filtering: captures subtle taste patterns humans wouldn't think to encode as features (people who buy X also buy surprisingly-unrelated Y), but is ==completely useless for a brand-new user or item with no interaction history==, the classic cold-start failure
- Content-based filtering: works immediately for new items the moment their metadata exists, and is easy to explain ('because you liked action movies'), but is limited to features someone thought to encode, and tends to over-recommend within a narrow lane instead of surfacing serendipitous cross-category picks
- Production systems blend both: collaborative filtering as the primary signal once enough interaction data exists, content-based similarity as the fallback and cold-start bridge, often combined in a single hybrid ranking model rather than kept as two separate systems

### The cold-start problem: recommending for a user or item with no history
A collaborative model has no embedding for a user or item it has never seen an interaction for, its dot-product math has nothing to multiply. For a new user, the fallback is typically catalog-wide **popularity** ('trending now') blended with any explicit onboarding signal (categories picked during signup), gradually replaced by personalized collaborative results as the user accumulates interactions. For a new item, the fallback is **content-based similarity** against items with an established interaction history, borrowing their embedding neighborhood until the new item earns its own interaction data.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Popularity-based fallback for new users: simple, always available, but generic, not personalized, and can create a rich-get-richer bias where already-popular items get shown even more
- Content-based fallback for new items: gets a new item into circulation immediately using its metadata, but is only as good as the quality of that metadata, and can misjudge items whose true audience isn't predictable from stated attributes alone
- A **hybrid ramp** is the real answer: weight the fallback heavily at zero history, and shift the blend toward the collaborative signal as real interactions accumulate for that specific user or item, rather than a hard cutover from one method to the other

### Offline model training vs online low-latency serving
Training a matrix factorization or embedding model over billions of interactions is a batch job that can reasonably take hours and run on a schedule (daily or hourly), it has no per-request latency requirement at all. Serving a recommendation, in contrast, happens on a page load and has a strict sub-200ms budget. Trying to do both in the same request path, computing a fresh recommendation from raw interaction data on every page view, is not viable at this scale, so the design deliberately splits them: heavy computation happens offline and its result is cached, the online path only ever does a cheap lookup plus a lightweight re-rank.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Fully online (compute-on-request) scoring: always maximally fresh, incorporates the very latest interaction, but far too slow and expensive to run the full model per request at this scale
- Fully offline (compute-once, serve-from-cache): fast and cheap to serve, but recommendations can be stale by up to a full training cycle (e.g. a full day) for interactions that happened after the last training run
- The real answer: precompute offline for the heavy lifting, then apply a cheap, real-time re-ranking pass online (boost items related to what the user clicked in this very session) to recover some freshness without paying the cost of full retraining per request

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The offline training job itself can become a multi-hour bottleneck as interaction volume grows; it's typically distributed across a cluster (matrix factorization frameworks that shard the computation by user or item block), and incremental training (updating embeddings from new data rather than fully retraining from scratch) becomes necessary well before daily retraining stops being affordable.
- The precomputed recommendation cache, read on nearly every page view, needs to be sharded by user_id across a distributed in-memory store, the same hot-path scaling concern as any other massive read-heavy cache.
- Popular items can dominate collaborative filtering results for everyone (a popularity bias baked into the embedding space itself); this is mitigated by explicitly down-weighting very-high-frequency items during training or diversity-boosting the final ranked list.
- As the catalog grows into the tens of millions of items, even the precomputed candidate generation step needs an approximate nearest-neighbor index over the embedding space (rather than a brute-force dot product against every item) to keep offline scoring tractable.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Proposing to compute recommendations from scratch on every page load==, missing that a matrix-factorization-style model is far too slow to run per request at this scale.
- ⚠️ Designing purely for existing users with rich histories and forgetting the cold-start case entirely, which an interviewer will almost certainly probe.
- ⚠️ Treating collaborative filtering and content-based filtering as an either/or choice instead of recognizing they solve different parts of the same problem (established users vs new entities).
- ⚠️ Not accounting for popularity bias, where a naive collaborative model just ends up recommending whatever's already popular to everyone, defeating the point of personalization.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't the recommendation model just be computed fresh for every request?**

> **Model Answer:** Matrix factorization or embedding-based scoring over a sparse matrix with billions of interactions is a batch computation that takes far longer than a request's latency budget allows. Splitting the design into an offline training pipeline (no latency constraint) and an online serving path that only does a cache lookup (strict latency constraint) is what makes both parts of the problem tractable.

**Q: How would you recommend items to a user who just signed up five minutes ago?**

> **Model Answer:** Fall back to a non-personalized or lightly-personalized signal: catalog-wide **popularity**, trending items, or category preferences captured during onboarding, and if the user has clicked on even one or two items in this session, blend in **content-based similarity** to those items. As real interaction history accumulates, the weighting gradually shifts toward the full collaborative model rather than switching over abruptly.

**Q: How do you keep a handful of extremely popular items from dominating every user's recommendation list?**

> **Model Answer:** Down-weight very-high-frequency items during training so their embeddings don't dominate the loss function, and apply a diversity or novelty boost when constructing the final ranked list, explicitly making room for less globally popular but well-matched items rather than optimizing purely for predicted engagement.

- Content-based fallback for new items: gets a new item into circulation immediately using its metadata, but is only as good as the quality of that metadata, and can misjudge items whose true audience isn't predictable from stated attributes alone
- A **hybrid ramp** is the real answer: weight the fallback heavily at zero history, and shift the blend toward the collaborative signal as real interactions accumulate for that specific user or item, rather than a hard cutover from one method to the other

### Offline model training vs online low-latency serving
Training a matrix factorization or embedding model over billions of interactions is a batch job that can reasonably take hours and run on a schedule (daily or hourly), it has no per-request latency requirement at all. Serving a recommendation, in contrast, happens on a page load and has a strict sub-200ms budget. Trying to do both in the same request path, computing a fresh recommendation from raw interaction data on every page view, is not viable at this scale, so the design deliberately splits them: heavy computation happens offline and its result is cached, the online path only ever does a cheap lookup plus a lightweight re-rank.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Fully online (compute-on-request) scoring: always maximally fresh, incorporates the very latest interaction, but far too slow and expensive to run the full model per request at this scale
- Fully offline (compute-once, serve-from-cache): fast and cheap to serve, but recommendations can be stale by up to a full training cycle (e.g. a full day) for interactions that happened after the last training run
- The real answer: precompute offline for the heavy lifting, then apply a cheap, real-time re-ranking pass online (boost items related to what the user clicked in this very session) to recover some freshness without paying the cost of full retraining per request

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The offline training job itself can become a multi-hour bottleneck as interaction volume grows; it's typically distributed across a cluster (matrix factorization frameworks that shard the computation by user or item block), and incremental training (updating embeddings from new data rather than fully retraining from scratch) becomes necessary well before daily retraining stops being affordable.
- The precomputed recommendation cache, read on nearly every page view, needs to be sharded by user_id across a distributed in-memory store, the same hot-path scaling concern as any other massive read-heavy cache.
- Popular items can dominate collaborative filtering results for everyone (a popularity bias baked into the embedding space itself); this is mitigated by explicitly down-weighting very-high-frequency items during training or diversity-boosting the final ranked list.
- As the catalog grows into the tens of millions of items, even the precomputed candidate generation step needs an approximate nearest-neighbor index over the embedding space (rather than a brute-force dot product against every item) to keep offline scoring tractable.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Proposing to compute recommendations from scratch on every page load==, missing that a matrix-factorization-style model is far too slow to run per request at this scale.
- ⚠️ Designing purely for existing users with rich histories and forgetting the cold-start case entirely, which an interviewer will almost certainly probe.
- ⚠️ Treating collaborative filtering and content-based filtering as an either/or choice instead of recognizing they solve different parts of the same problem (established users vs new entities).
- ⚠️ Not accounting for popularity bias, where a naive collaborative model just ends up recommending whatever's already popular to everyone, defeating the point of personalization.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't the recommendation model just be computed fresh for every request?**

> **Model Answer:** Matrix factorization or embedding-based scoring over a sparse matrix with billions of interactions is a batch computation that takes far longer than a request's latency budget allows. Splitting the design into an offline training pipeline (no latency constraint) and an online serving path that only does a cache lookup (strict latency constraint) is what makes both parts of the problem tractable.

**Q: How would you recommend items to a user who just signed up five minutes ago?**

> **Model Answer:** Fall back to a non-personalized or lightly-personalized signal: catalog-wide **popularity**, trending items, or category preferences captured during onboarding, and if the user has clicked on even one or two items in this session, blend in **content-based similarity** to those items. As real interaction history accumulates, the weighting gradually shifts toward the full collaborative model rather than switching over abruptly.

**Q: How do you keep a handful of extremely popular items from dominating every user's recommendation list?**

> **Model Answer:** Down-weight very-high-frequency items during training so their embeddings don't dominate the loss function, and apply a diversity or novelty boost when constructing the final ranked list, explicitly making room for less globally popular but well-matched items rather than optimizing purely for predicted engagement.

# Design an E-commerce Product Search & Filtering System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Amazon • eBay` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This isn't a text-search problem wearing a shopping costume, it's two different query types glued together at the hip: **free-text relevance matching** (how well does 'wireless headphones' match this product) and **structured faceted filtering** (show me only the ones under $50 that are in stock), and the ranking that actually sells product has to blend both with real business signals, ==not just text similarity==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the search experience for a large e-commerce site: a user types a
query like "wireless headphones", gets back a ranked list of matching
products, and can then narrow that list using filters like brand, price
range, color, rating, and in-stock status, all without a full page reload.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How large is the product catalog, and how often does it change (new listings, price updates, stock changes)?
*Why it matters:* A catalog of a few million SKUs with prices and stock counts changing constantly needs a search index that supports frequent updates, not just a slow nightly rebuild, which shapes the whole indexing pipeline.

#### Q: What filters need to be supported, and are they fixed per category or do sellers define custom attributes?
*Why it matters:* A fixed set of filters (price, brand, rating) is a straightforward faceted query. Seller-defined custom attributes (screen size for laptops, but not for t-shirts) mean the index schema itself needs to be dynamic per category, which is a materially different indexing problem.

#### Q: What should ranking optimize for, pure text relevance, or business outcomes like conversion and revenue?
*Why it matters:* A search engine that ranks purely by text match will happily put an out-of-stock, poorly-reviewed item above an in-stock bestseller if the text matches slightly better. E-commerce search almost always blends relevance with business signals, and that decision changes the whole ranking model.

#### Q: Do filter counts need to update live as a user applies filters (e.g. 'Brand: Sony (482)') or is an approximate count acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Exact live facet counts over a huge, filtered result set is a nontrivial aggregation cost per query. If approximate or slightly cached counts are acceptable, that opens up much cheaper caching strategies.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can enter a free-text query and get back a ranked list of matching products.
- A user can apply one or more filters (brand, price range, category, color, rating, in-stock) to narrow the current result set.
- The results page shows facet options with counts (e.g. how many results exist per brand) reflecting the currently applied filters.
- The product index reflects catalog changes (new listings, price and stock updates) within a bounded, reasonably short delay.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Search and filter queries must return in well under a second, ideally under 200-300ms, since latency directly affects conversion rate on a shopping site.**
- **The system must scale to tens of millions of SKUs and tens of thousands of queries per second at peak (e.g. holiday shopping traffic).**
- **High availability for the search path, since a broken or unavailable search bar effectively takes down product discovery for the entire site.**
- **Freshness matters for price and stock in particular, showing an out-of-stock or wrong-priced item as available is a direct trust and revenue problem, more urgent than general catalog freshness.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50 million active SKUs in the catalog
- Average product document (title, description, attributes, price, stock) is about 2KB once indexed
- 200 million search queries per day
- 10% of SKUs (5 million) have a price or stock change on a typical day

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total index size:** 50,000,000 SKUs * 2KB ≈ 100GB of indexed document data, well within reach of a modestly sized sharded cluster, not a distributed-systems-scale problem on its own
- **Query throughput:** 200,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 2,300 queries/sec average, with peak shopping traffic commonly 5-10x that, so design for roughly 15,000-20,000 queries/sec at peak
- **Near-real-time update rate:** 5,000,000 changed SKUs/day / 86,400 seconds ≈ 58 updates/sec average, small compared to query volume, meaning the index must support concurrent reads and writes but isn't write-bound
- **Facet aggregation cost:** A single query with 5 active filters against a 50-million-document index needs the search engine to aggregate counts per facet value across the matched subset, which is what makes faceted search meaningfully more expensive per query than plain keyword search

*Capacity Takeaway:* The catalog itself is modest in size (100GB, tens of millions of SKUs), so the real cost driver isn't index size, it's query complexity: every query does full-text matching AND structured filtering AND facet-count aggregation in one request, which is why an inverted-index engine built for exactly this combined workload (like Elasticsearch or Solr) is the standard answer rather than a plain relational database.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
The catalog service remains the system of record for product data; every
create, price change, or stock update publishes an event that an indexing
pipeline consumes and upserts into a sharded, inverted-index-backed search
cluster (product_index), keeping the index a near-real-time, eventually
consistent derived copy of the catalog. A search request carries both a
free-text query and a structured filter set in one call; the search engine
resolves the text portion against its inverted index for relevance
candidates, applies the structured filters (brand, price range, in_stock)
as a fast exact-match/range narrowing step over that candidate set, computes
facet counts over the narrowed set for the filter sidebar, and returns a
ranked page blending text relevance with business signals like sales rank
and in-stock status. This combined text-plus-structured workload is exactly
why the underlying engine is a dedicated inverted-index search technology
rather than a general-purpose relational database.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Catalog-to-index pipeline and query path

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    events>"Update Events"]:::queue
    indexer["Indexing Worker"]:::server
    searchindex["Sharded Product Index"]:::server
    client["Client"]:::client
    gateway["API Gateway"]:::server
    searchsvc["Search Service"]:::server

    gateway --> searchsvc
    searchsvc -->|"text + filter query"| searchindex
    searchindex -->|"ranked results + facets"| searchsvc
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search` | Query params: q (search text), filters (structured, e.g. brand=Sony&price_max=50&in_stock=true), sort, page. Returns ranked, paginated products plus facet counts for the current result set. |
| `GET` | `/api/search/facets` | Query params: q, filters (same as above). Returns just the facet breakdown (brand counts, price buckets, etc.) for the current query and filter state, used to render/update the filter sidebar without re-fetching the full result list. |
| `POST` | `/internal/catalog/product` | Internal-only. Called by the catalog service on a product create/update (price, stock, attributes) to upsert that product into the search index. |
| `DELETE` | `/internal/catalog/product/{productId}` | Internal-only. Removes a delisted product from the search index. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `product_index`
- `product_id (unique)`
- `title, description (full-text indexed fields)`
- `brand, category, color (exact-match filterable fields)`
- `price (numeric, range-filterable)`
- `rating_avg, rating_count`
- `in_stock (boolean)`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* The actual search-engine document, not a normal relational row, a combination of full-text-indexed fields (title, description) and separately indexed structured fields used purely for filtering and faceting (brand, price, in_stock), which is exactly what an inverted-index search engine is built to do in one query.

### Entity: `catalog_master`
- `product_id (unique)`
- `seller_id`
- `full attribute set`
- `current price, current stock count`
*Notes:* The source of truth for product data, owned by the catalog/inventory service, not the search system; the search index is a derived, denormalized, eventually-consistent copy optimized for query speed, not a system of record.

### Entity: `query_log`
- `query_text`
- `filters_applied`
- `result_count`
- `clicked_product_id (nullable)`
- `timestamp`
*Notes:* Feeds ranking improvements and business analytics (which queries return zero results, which filters get abandoned), not part of the live query path.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Full-text relevance vs structured faceted filtering, handled in one query
Full-text search asks 'how well does this document match these words', scored with something like BM25, tolerant of word order and partial matches. Faceted filtering asks a completely different kind of question: 'is this field's value exactly Sony, or between $20 and $50, or true', a hard boolean constraint, not a fuzzy score. A single product search query needs to do both at once: text-match relevance ranking over the fields that matter for meaning (title, description), and hard filtering over the fields that matter for narrowing (brand, price, stock), then aggregate counts per facet value over whatever survived the filtering. This dual nature is exactly what inverted-index engines like Elasticsearch or Solr are purpose-built for, combining a text-scoring query language with structured filter clauses in one request.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Doing text search and structured filtering as two separate systems (a search engine for text, a relational database for structured filters, joined in application code): avoids vendor lock-in to one engine, but requires an expensive application-level join/intersection on every query, which doesn't scale to tens of thousands of queries per second
- Doing both inside one inverted-index engine (structured fields indexed alongside text fields, filters expressed as query clauses): a single fast query per search, but requires committing to a search-engine-specific schema and query language rather than plain SQL
- The real answer at this scale: one inverted-index engine, structured fields indexed as filterable/aggregatable (not analyzed like text), letting one query resolve relevance, filtering, and facet counts together, which is the standard e-commerce search architecture

### Ranking: blending text relevance with business signals
A pure text-relevance score (BM25-style) treats 'wireless headphones' matching a product title as the whole story, but a search engine that ranks a discontinued, out-of-stock item above an identical in-stock bestseller because its title happens to match slightly better is optimizing for the wrong thing. Production e-commerce ranking combines text relevance with business signals: in-stock status (often a hard filter or a heavy ranking penalty), sales rank or conversion rate (items that actually sell when shown get boosted), rating, and sometimes sponsored placement, into one final score.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure text relevance only: simple, purely a function of query and document text, but frequently surfaces poor business outcomes (out-of-stock items, low-quality listings that happen to match the words well)
- Heavily business-signal-weighted ranking: drives better conversion and revenue, but can feel 'wrong' to users if it overrides obvious text relevance too aggressively (a barely-related bestseller outranking an exact-match niche item)
- The real answer: text relevance sets the initial candidate set and base score, business signals apply as a bounded boost/penalty on top rather than dominating the score outright, keeping results feeling relevant while still favoring items that convert

### Faceted filter counts: computing them fast without scanning the whole catalog per query
Rendering a filter sidebar like 'Brand: Sony (482), Bose (310)...' requires counting, for each candidate facet value, how many documents in the current filtered result set have that value, an aggregation over potentially millions of matching documents on every keystroke or filter click. Inverted-index engines support this efficiently because each indexed field already has its own postings structure, so counting documents per facet value within a filtered set is a structure the engine is built for, not a full table scan, but it's still real per-query work that scales with result-set size and facet cardinality.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Computing exact facet counts on every query: always accurate, but adds real aggregation cost per query, especially with several high-cardinality facets (like brand, with thousands of distinct values) active at once
- Capping facet aggregation to the top-K most frequent values per field and accepting approximate counts beyond that: much cheaper, and the long tail of rarely-selected facet values rarely matters to users anyway
- Caching facet aggregations for extremely common query-plus-filter combinations (e.g. a popular category landing page with no filters yet applied): near-free on cache hit, but requires invalidation whenever underlying stock or price changes shift the counts meaningfully

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Popular category or query terms create hot shards in the search cluster during peak shopping events; mitigated the same way as any hot-shard problem, replicating hot shards more heavily and caching full result pages for the most common query-and-filter combinations.
- Price and stock updates need a near-real-time path from the catalog service into the index (an event stream feeding an indexing worker), a slow batch-only index refresh would show stale prices and sell out-of-stock items, an unacceptable trust problem for this domain specifically.
- High-cardinality facets (like 'seller' with hundreds of thousands of distinct values, or seller-defined custom attributes) can blow up facet aggregation cost; capping displayed facet values and treating rarely-used custom attributes as non-faceted or lazily computed keeps this bounded.
- As the catalog grows and query volume spikes seasonally (holiday shopping), the search cluster needs to scale shard replicas elastically ahead of known-traffic events rather than reactively during an incident.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Modeling this as a plain relational database with a LIKE '%query%' clause, which cannot deliver real relevance ranking or efficient faceted aggregation at scale.
- ⚠️ Designing ranking as pure text relevance and ignoring in-stock status and business signals entirely, producing technically-correct but commercially-bad results.
- ⚠️ Treating the search index and the catalog database as the same system, instead of recognizing the index is a derived, denormalized, eventually-consistent copy that needs its own sync pipeline.
- ⚠️ Assuming facet counts are free to compute, when in reality they're real aggregation work that scales with result-set size and facet cardinality and needs its own scaling consideration.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why not just run this on a relational database with indexed columns and a LIKE query?**

> **Model Answer:** A relational LIKE query can't do real relevance scoring (ranking by how well a document matches, not just whether it contains the substring), can't efficiently tokenize and rank free text, and doing faceted aggregation over millions of rows per query would require expensive GROUP BY operations that don't scale to tens of thousands of queries per second. Inverted-index search engines are purpose-built for exactly this combined text-plus-structured-plus-aggregation workload.

**Q: How would you make sure an item that just sold out doesn't keep showing as available in search results?**

> **Model Answer:** Treat stock and price changes as high-priority events on a near-real-time path from the catalog service into the search index, rather than relying on a periodic batch reindex, since showing a wrong price or sold-out item as available is a direct trust and revenue problem, more urgent than general catalog freshness like a description update.

**Q: A user applies five filters and the facet sidebar takes 800ms to update, what would you look at first?**

> **Model Answer:** Check whether facet aggregation is being computed exactly across the full narrowed result set on every field, including high-cardinality ones; capping aggregation to the top-K most common values per facet field and caching aggregations for common filter combinations typically recovers most of that latency without materially hurting the sidebar's usefulness.

- `seller_id`
- `full attribute set`
- `current price, current stock count`
*Notes:* The source of truth for product data, owned by the catalog/inventory service, not the search system; the search index is a derived, denormalized, eventually-consistent copy optimized for query speed, not a system of record.

### Entity: `query_log`
- `query_text`
- `filters_applied`
- `result_count`
- `clicked_product_id (nullable)`
- `timestamp`
*Notes:* Feeds ranking improvements and business analytics (which queries return zero results, which filters get abandoned), not part of the live query path.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Full-text relevance vs structured faceted filtering, handled in one query
Full-text search asks 'how well does this document match these words', scored with something like BM25, tolerant of word order and partial matches. Faceted filtering asks a completely different kind of question: 'is this field's value exactly Sony, or between $20 and $50, or true', a hard boolean constraint, not a fuzzy score. A single product search query needs to do both at once: text-match relevance ranking over the fields that matter for meaning (title, description), and hard filtering over the fields that matter for narrowing (brand, price, stock), then aggregate counts per facet value over whatever survived the filtering. This dual nature is exactly what inverted-index engines like Elasticsearch or Solr are purpose-built for, combining a text-scoring query language with structured filter clauses in one request.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Doing text search and structured filtering as two separate systems (a search engine for text, a relational database for structured filters, joined in application code): avoids vendor lock-in to one engine, but requires an expensive application-level join/intersection on every query, which doesn't scale to tens of thousands of queries per second
- Doing both inside one inverted-index engine (structured fields indexed alongside text fields, filters expressed as query clauses): a single fast query per search, but requires committing to a search-engine-specific schema and query language rather than plain SQL
- The real answer at this scale: one inverted-index engine, structured fields indexed as filterable/aggregatable (not analyzed like text), letting one query resolve relevance, filtering, and facet counts together, which is the standard e-commerce search architecture

### Ranking: blending text relevance with business signals
A pure text-relevance score (BM25-style) treats 'wireless headphones' matching a product title as the whole story, but a search engine that ranks a discontinued, out-of-stock item above an identical in-stock bestseller because its title happens to match slightly better is optimizing for the wrong thing. Production e-commerce ranking combines text relevance with business signals: in-stock status (often a hard filter or a heavy ranking penalty), sales rank or conversion rate (items that actually sell when shown get boosted), rating, and sometimes sponsored placement, into one final score.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure text relevance only: simple, purely a function of query and document text, but frequently surfaces poor business outcomes (out-of-stock items, low-quality listings that happen to match the words well)
- Heavily business-signal-weighted ranking: drives better conversion and revenue, but can feel 'wrong' to users if it overrides obvious text relevance too aggressively (a barely-related bestseller outranking an exact-match niche item)
- The real answer: text relevance sets the initial candidate set and base score, business signals apply as a bounded boost/penalty on top rather than dominating the score outright, keeping results feeling relevant while still favoring items that convert

### Faceted filter counts: computing them fast without scanning the whole catalog per query
Rendering a filter sidebar like 'Brand: Sony (482), Bose (310)...' requires counting, for each candidate facet value, how many documents in the current filtered result set have that value, an aggregation over potentially millions of matching documents on every keystroke or filter click. Inverted-index engines support this efficiently because each indexed field already has its own postings structure, so counting documents per facet value within a filtered set is a structure the engine is built for, not a full table scan, but it's still real per-query work that scales with result-set size and facet cardinality.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Computing exact facet counts on every query: always accurate, but adds real aggregation cost per query, especially with several high-cardinality facets (like brand, with thousands of distinct values) active at once
- Capping facet aggregation to the top-K most frequent values per field and accepting approximate counts beyond that: much cheaper, and the long tail of rarely-selected facet values rarely matters to users anyway
- Caching facet aggregations for extremely common query-plus-filter combinations (e.g. a popular category landing page with no filters yet applied): near-free on cache hit, but requires invalidation whenever underlying stock or price changes shift the counts meaningfully

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Popular category or query terms create hot shards in the search cluster during peak shopping events; mitigated the same way as any hot-shard problem, replicating hot shards more heavily and caching full result pages for the most common query-and-filter combinations.
- Price and stock updates need a near-real-time path from the catalog service into the index (an event stream feeding an indexing worker), a slow batch-only index refresh would show stale prices and sell out-of-stock items, an unacceptable trust problem for this domain specifically.
- High-cardinality facets (like 'seller' with hundreds of thousands of distinct values, or seller-defined custom attributes) can blow up facet aggregation cost; capping displayed facet values and treating rarely-used custom attributes as non-faceted or lazily computed keeps this bounded.
- As the catalog grows and query volume spikes seasonally (holiday shopping), the search cluster needs to scale shard replicas elastically ahead of known-traffic events rather than reactively during an incident.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Modeling this as a plain relational database with a LIKE '%query%' clause, which cannot deliver real relevance ranking or efficient faceted aggregation at scale.
- ⚠️ Designing ranking as pure text relevance and ignoring in-stock status and business signals entirely, producing technically-correct but commercially-bad results.
- ⚠️ Treating the search index and the catalog database as the same system, instead of recognizing the index is a derived, denormalized, eventually-consistent copy that needs its own sync pipeline.
- ⚠️ Assuming facet counts are free to compute, when in reality they're real aggregation work that scales with result-set size and facet cardinality and needs its own scaling consideration.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why not just run this on a relational database with indexed columns and a LIKE query?**

> **Model Answer:** A relational LIKE query can't do real relevance scoring (ranking by how well a document matches, not just whether it contains the substring), can't efficiently tokenize and rank free text, and doing faceted aggregation over millions of rows per query would require expensive GROUP BY operations that don't scale to tens of thousands of queries per second. Inverted-index search engines are purpose-built for exactly this combined text-plus-structured-plus-aggregation workload.

**Q: How would you make sure an item that just sold out doesn't keep showing as available in search results?**

> **Model Answer:** Treat stock and price changes as high-priority events on a near-real-time path from the catalog service into the search index, rather than relying on a periodic batch reindex, since showing a wrong price or sold-out item as available is a direct trust and revenue problem, more urgent than general catalog freshness like a description update.

**Q: A user applies five filters and the facet sidebar takes 800ms to update, what would you look at first?**

> **Model Answer:** Check whether facet aggregation is being computed exactly across the full narrowed result set on every field, including high-cardinality ones; capping aggregation to the top-K most common values per facet field and caching aggregations for common filter combinations typically recovers most of that latency without materially hurting the sidebar's usefulness.
